reason: Attacked on all four fronts and it held. WORDING: I fetched the Perseus English card 426 of Euripides, Suppliants, whose header credits The Complete Greek Drama, ed. Oates and O'Neill, Random House, 1938, trans. E. P. Coleridge; it prints the sentence exactly as proposed, rich and weak alike have equal justice, with the marginal [435] falling immediately after it. I then fetched the Internet Classics Archive copy of the same Coleridge translation, which reads rich and poor alike have equal justice. So the two states the note describes are real and the proposal quotes the one it names. The Greek settles which reading is faithful: line 433 is the weak, ho t' asthenes, and line 434 is the rich, ho plousios, so weak is the literal word and poor is the looser Bohn rendering, not the other way round. LOCATOR: I asked the Perseus Greek card 426 where its marginal numbers fall. 430 sits beside hopou to men protiston ouk eisin nomoi; counting down, gegrammenon de ton nomon ho t' asthenes is 433 and ho plousios te ten diken isen echei is 434, with 435 beside estin d' enispein toisin asthenesterois. The quoted sentence is exactly lines 433 to 434, as claimed. An earlier summariser reading of the same page returned 432 to 433; the marginal-number check overrides it and agrees with the English card. SPEAKER: both the Greek and the English pages name Theseus, replying to the Theban herald in the democracy speech. ATTRIBUTION: not on the misattribution list, no minting, the cut at a complete clause with a full stop is disclosed in the note and matches accepted practice elsewhere in the carry. SHIPPED/CAP: shipped.js returns no shipped line, no near opener, Euripides at 1 for the year from month 6, not banned, not at cap, and no Euripides among the September carry-ins, so no person twice in the month. FORMAT: source is 84 characters, leads with the author, work then locator then speaker then translation in parentheses, no dash, no straight double quote, quotation ends in a full stop, tag Drama is the form of the work. SCOPE: pre-2000 drama, on the theme of what is owed, publishable. One residual, not a refutation: the year 1938 is the year of the printing whose wording is used, which is what the rule asks for, but on its own it can be read as claiming Coleridge translated in 1938 when his version is of 1891. Naming the volume removes that reading and still fits inside 140 characters, so I offer it below as a better source line rather than a correction.
betterCitation: Euripides, The Suppliants, lines 433 to 434 (Theseus) (trans. E. P. Coleridge, Random House, 1938)
